We introduced Minimum Intervention Reweighting, a dual-constraint framework for contamination-aware pretraining that derives per-batch exponents $\bstar$ without validation data.
The method finds the smallest $b$ satisfying $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, enforcing a minimum intervention principle: apply only as much downweighting as needed to meet a quality floor, no more.

At 0.6B scale with 40\% synthetic contamination, adaptive $\bstar$ achieves comparable performance to grid-search-optimal $b{=}0.3$ (PPL 17.653 vs.\ 17.640; gap 0.013, within range of cross-seed variance ${\sim}0.007$), capturing ${\sim}76\%$ of the grid-best improvement over uniform (17.694) while eliminating the grid search entirely.
Hard filtering (Detect \& Remove at $q{>}0.5$) achieves lower PPL (17.290) due to direct distribution match with the human-authored evaluation set, but requires a calibrated detection threshold that reweighting avoids.
ESS-only maximum intervention (PPL $17.723 {\pm} 0.006$) provides no improvement over uniform, confirming that minimum intervention is the better operating point.
At $\rho = 0.6$, adaptive $\bstar$ maintains its advantage over uniform (17.740 vs.\ 17.766), though the gap narrows and degradation is faster than for fixed-$b$ methods ($+$0.087 vs.\ $+$0.053 for grid $b{=}0.5$), suggesting that $\tau$ may benefit from light per-$\rho$ adjustment.
The quality threshold $\tau$ is robust across $[0.5, 0.8]$---all values in this range improve over uniform---and a lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices when calibrated (ECE\,=\,0.048).

Our evaluation is limited to a single model scale (0.6B) and controlled injection setting.
Whether the calibration-over-discrimination observation generalizes remains a hypothesis pending multi-detector comparison.

Three directions merit investigation: (1)~scaling to larger models (3B+) to test whether $\tau$ and $\nmin$ defaults transfer across scales; (2)~controlled comparison across multiple detector families to verify the calibration hypothesis; (3)~evaluation on naturally contaminated web corpora where ground-truth provenance labels are unavailable.

We introduced Minimum Intervention Reweighting, a dual-constraint framework that derives per-batch exponents $\bstar$ without validation data by finding the smallest $b$ satisfying $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$.

At 0.6B scale with 40\% contamination, adaptive $\bstar$ approximates grid-best within 0.013 PPL (17.653 vs.\ 17.640) while eliminating grid search entirely.
ESS-only maximum intervention provides no improvement over uniform, confirming minimum intervention as the better operating point.
Hard filtering achieves lower absolute PPL (17.290) but requires threshold calibration that reweighting avoids.
At $\rho{=}0.6$, the advantage narrows ($+$0.087 degradation vs.\ $+$0.053 for grid $b{=}0.5$), suggesting $\tau$ benefits from per-$\rho$ adjustment ($\tau \in [0.7, 0.8]$ optimal across tested levels).
A lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout.

Future work: scaling to 3B+ models, multi-detector comparison to test the calibration hypothesis, and evaluation on naturally contaminated corpora.

\paragraph{Reweighting vs.\ hard filtering.}
Detect \& Remove achieves the lowest PPL (17.290), outperforming all reweighting methods by ${\geq}0.35$---a gap arising from distribution match: the evaluation set is purely human-authored, so filtering aligns training with evaluation more directly than reweighting can.
However, filtering requires a calibrated threshold ($q{>}0.5$); misspecification discards real data or retains contamination.
Adaptive reweighting avoids this binary decision: $\bstar$ adjusts continuously without a threshold, closing ${\sim}76\%$ of the gap to grid-searched optimum at zero validation cost.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Method selection as a spectrum.}
The methods form a spectrum of aggressiveness vs.\ safety.
Detect \& Remove achieves the lowest PPL (17.290 at $q{>}0.5$, 17.253 at $q{>}0.3$) but requires precise threshold calibration---and there is no principled way to choose between thresholds without validation data.
A hybrid approach (conservative filtering at $q{>}0.95$ followed by adaptive reweighting on the remainder) achieves PPL 17.514, intermediate between pure filtering and pure reweighting (Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}).
Adaptive reweighting (17.653) is threshold-free and retains all data, making it the safest choice when detection quality is uncertain or data is scarce.
These are not competing methods but points on a single trade-off: aggressiveness yields lower PPL when the detector is well-calibrated, while conservatism provides robustness when it is not.

124	Convergence theory for contaminated training shows that convergence rate improves with the effective real fraction~\citep{wang2026survive}, motivating a lower bound on $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
125	The specific value of $\tau$ is set empirically.
126	We find a wide safe range: $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ consistently outperforms uniform training (Section~\ref{sec:results}), with $\tau = 0.8$ achieving the best perplexity.
127	Above 0.8, $b^{*}$ inflates rapidly (mean $b^{*} = 3.08$ at $\tau = 0.95$), causing over-downweighting.
128	We use $\tau = 0.8$ as the default throughout.

tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{ESS floor $n_{\min}$.}
We recommend $n_{\min} = \max(2, \lfloor B/2 \rfloor)$ as a default that scales with batch size without manual tuning.
At this ratio, the ESS ceiling binds on a majority of batches (providing gradient stability) while leaving room for $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ to determine $b^{*}$ in the remainder (enabling quality-driven intervention).
Ratios below ${\sim}1/4$ effectively remove the stability constraint ($n_{\min}{=}1$, $B{=}4$: mean $b^{*}$ rises to 7.20, PPL degrades by $+$0.14), while $n_{\min}/B{=}1$ prevents intervention entirely ($b^{*} \equiv 0$, recovering uniform training).
This default is validated at $B \in \{4, 8\}$ (Section~\ref{sec:sensitivity}); we leave fine-grained ratio characterization (e.g., $0.4$ vs.\ $0.6$) to future work.
